A call a tool refused is marked differently from one that failed, and each turn shows what it cost, with the share the provider served from its cache in the ledger.

title: The health check finds what a model hides
details: Beyond missing units and unlinked flows it now names the three faults that survive review: double counting, where the same burden enters twice by two routes; exchanges pointing the wrong way; and mass that appears out of nowhere, where a process puts out more than it takes in. Each finding quotes the number behind it, so there is nothing to chase that is not backed by a figure.

title: Reports: a document you keep, not a look you take
details: Short reports are the quick look and store nothing. A full report is a document: it keeps its own name, language, theme, variants, indicators and chapter list, so you re-render it when the numbers change, and one model can hold several. It starts with the chapters ISO 14044 asks for, arranges them by drag, takes structural templates you bring, and comes out as a typeset PDF in five languages or a Typst project.

title: The assistant writes a chapter — after investigating
details: A chapter is written after the assistant has queried the results, the inventory and the study metadata, so it cites what the model says. You can edit the prompt behind any chapter and comment on what it wrote for a rewrite; a refused chapter is kept as a draft, and writing can be cancelled mid-run. Bold, italics and lists survive into the typeset page, and each writer knows which tables and figures are printed with its chapter.

title: Numbers in a report are never typed out
details: Every figure in a chapter comes from the calculation, not from the model writing it down: the report does the arithmetic a comparison needs — differences, shares, percentages against a reference — and prints numbers with the precision the data actually support rather than a fixed number of decimals. Charts follow the same rule.

title: What an LCA may not claim, checked
details: ISO 14044 forbids a comparative assertion built on aggregated indicators, and forbids calling a single-indicator result an LCA. A check reads what each chapter claims — not just the numbers it quotes — and flags the sentence that oversteps, covering the three interpretation checks (completeness, sensitivity, consistency) and the limitations note you cannot drop from a comparative study.

title: The parts a study needs, kept up to date
details: A bibliography that cites the datasets and methods the report actually used, a glossary that grows with the document, and an abbreviations chapter resolved for you. The annex takes its inventory length on the chapter itself — 25 rows by default, the largest by contribution, or every characterised flow of the reference process, which on an ecoinvent model is a few thousand rows and tens of pages. Elementary flows are in the export in full.

title: Contribution analysis compares your variants
details: The contribution tree carries every variant side by side, and a click on any node opens that process's details without leaving the page. The chart is grouped by default — the groups on the axis, one bar per variant, and a bold Total group carrying each variant's sum — or stacked, which turns it round and shows the composition at a glance.

title: The assistant works in batches, and by name
details: Instead of one call per exchange it edits in batches, addresses processes by name rather than by internal id, and reports what it changed as a list. A cradle-to-grave model with every transport genuinely takes a few hundred calls; when the round budget runs out it stops and says so, and you tell it to continue.

title: Processes and exchanges carry their documentation
details: A foreground process takes a description, and an exchange takes a comment — where the number came from, which assumption it rests on, what was excluded. Two allocation decisions are recorded per process, which is what a reviewer asks for first and what the report prints in its methods chapter.

title: Scenarios: your own, from Excel, and in the results
details: A scenario is a named set of parameter overrides, stored with the model, edited as you type, and importable from an Excel workbook — where every cell is validated before anything is written, so a bad sheet changes nothing. Tick any number of them on Results or Detailed results to compare them against each other and against the untouched model.

title: The assistant researches what the databases cannot give you
details: End-of-life split rates, material compositions, transport distances: a separate helper searches the web and returns short findings, each with a source URL, and drops what it cannot source instead of estimating. Describe a product without composition data and it researches the bill of materials against the total mass; it can also review a finished model, with a second reviewer challenging it.

title: A cost limit, and a ledger to check it against
details: One run may spend at most what you set (default $2; 0 switches it off) — helper runs count towards the same limit, and the assistant stops and says so when it is reached. A reply-length cap is the backstop the cost limit cannot be, since that one settles up between tool rounds. Costs shows real spend per model and month.

title: Create your own LCIA methods, and inspect the factors
details: Build a method from characterization factors of your own, or from a shipped one you adjust, and use it like any other. The LCIA page shows the factors behind a method and compares two of them side by side, which is how you find out why two “climate change” variants disagree. Recommended indicators are marked, so a first calculation does not start with a shopping list.

title: Workspaces, models, and an Overview to start from
details: Create and delete workspaces, duplicate a model to try a variant without touching the original, and compare subjects across models in one calculation. The Overview page opens on your models with their size and their reference process, the study's progress, and this feed.

title: Tags, and results split by the life cycle
details: Tag processes freely — life-cycle phase, site, supplier, anything — and split or group any chart and any contribution breakdown by a tag family. Elementary-flow contributions are shown per flow and exported to Excel. Only families actually in use are offered, so a split never draws one bar called untagged.

title: The canvas handles like a diagram tool
details: Right-click to add a process where you clicked, select several nodes at once, read each arrow's unit on the arrow, and keep flow lists sorted the way you left them. Units autocomplete, and strict mode refuses a typo like “KG” unless you deliberately allow free text. Canvas references survive a restart.

title: Voice input for the chat
details: Dictate instead of typing; the recording is transcribed automatically. Pin your spoken language so a German sentence is not quietly translated to English.

title: Skills the assistant follows
details: Knowledge sheets rather than one long prompt: goal & scope, model building, choosing a proxy dataset, parameters & formulas, bills of materials, end-of-life, interpreting results, critical review. The built-in ones ship with the app and can be read in full; add your own house rules as a new skill.

title: An assistant inside the app
details: A chat beside the canvas that can actually build: it searches datasets, adds and connects processes, sets parameters, calculates, tags, and reads the results back to you — through the same API and the same validation your own clicks go through, so everything it does is audited and undoable.
